extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: A benchmark of 11.5K college-level multimodal questions across 30 subjects and 6 disciplines for evaluating multimodal understanding and reasoning.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue; Yuansheng Ni; Kai Zhang; Tianyu Zheng; Ruoqi Liu; Ge Zhang; Samuel Stevens; Dongfu Jiang; Weiming Ren; Yuxuan Sun; Cong Wei; Botao Yu; Ruibin Yuan; Renliang Sun; Ming Yin; Boyuan Zheng; Zhenzhu Yang; Yibo Liu; Wenhao Huang; Huan Sun; Yu Su; Wenhu Chen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was curated in stages by selecting subjects with useful visual inputs, recruiting over 50 university students including co-authors to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources, and creating new questions when necessary, followed by cleaning, formatting, and difficulty filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: College exams, quizzes, textbooks, online sources, and lecture materials.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Potential duplicates were identified using lexical overlap and source URL similarity and reviewed by authors; problems were then checked for format and typos, categorized by difficulty, and about 10% labeled very easy were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and created new questions when necessary; authors later reviewed duplicates, formatting, typos, and difficulty.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Authors reviewed suspected duplicates, checked formatting and typos, and categorized problems into four difficulty levels, excluding about 10% that were too easy.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in various disciplines and subjects.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is motivated by monitoring progress toward Expert AGI because such systems could substitute for skilled adult labor and pose risks of job displacement and economic disruption.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark may carry biases from manual curation, focuses on college-level subjects, and is not sufficient by itself to test Expert AGI or map to the 90th percentile of skilled adults.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating multimodal models in zero-shot, few-shot development, validation, and test settings; the dataset is divided into development, validation, and test sets.

name.evidence: We introduce the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning (MMMU) benchmark

description.evidence: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Data Collection. Our benchmark collection takes three stages. Firstly, we go through the common university majors to decide what subjects should be included in our benchmark. ... In the second stage, we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection. They collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The questions in our benchmark were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To further control the quality of our data, we perform two steps of data cleaning. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking. ... In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: In the second stage, we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection. They collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: It denotes an AI system that reaches “at least 90th percentile of skilled adults” in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve “the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor” for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. Therefore, it is of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor the progress towards Expert AGI.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI [57].

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: MMMU, constituting 11.5K questions, is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set, and a test set. The few-shot development set includes 5 questions per subject, and the validation set, useful for hyperparameter selection, contains approximately 900 questions, while the test set comprises 10.5K questions.
